chapter.title: Rexx Classes and .NET Classes
chapter.para: A Rexx class can stand for .NET objects in two ways. A subclass of NetObject is a Rexx view of a .NET object, which .NET does not know about: its methods come first for Rexx code. A Rexx class that extends a .NET class is a .NET class too: .NET calls its methods where it would call the overrides of a C# subclass, so a Rexx class can be a Windows Forms Form with its own OnPaint, an IComparer for .NET's sorts, or an INotifyPropertyChanged for WPF's binding.

section.title: Subclasses of NetObject
section.para: .MyClass~new(o), with MyClass a subclass of NetObject (or of NetArray) and o a NetObject, is an object of MyClass that stands for the same .NET object: one more proxy, == to o, which goes to .NET as that object. As in any Rexx class, its methods come first, and its unknown, if it has one, gets every other message, and reaches .NET with FORWARD CLASS (SUPER); a name that nothing handles is SYNTAX 97.1. Its own init must call self~init:super(o). The subclass is a view chosen by Rexx code: the same .NET object, coming back from .NET later, is a plain NetObject again.

example.title: A Rexx subclass of NetObject
example.programlisting:
sb = .Loud~new(.net~System~Text~StringBuilder~new("abc")) say sb~Shout sb~Length say sb == sb~Append("d")
::requires "net.cls" ::class Loud subclass NetObject ::method unknown use arg name, args if name = "SHOUT" then return self~ToString~upper forward class (super)

section.title: Extending a .NET Class
section.para: .net~extend(.MyClass, base [, interface...]), once per class (the class's activate class method is the natural place), with MyClass a subclass of NetObject, makes a .NET type that derives from base (a class; or, for an interface, System.Object) and implements the interfaces, and returns it, a NetType (). Every member of the base that can be overridden (virtual or abstract, public or protected, not sealed) and every member of the interfaces (and of the interfaces they extend) that MyClass has a method for, counting its superclasses below NetObject, is overridden by that method:

listitem.para: A method is overridden by the Rexx method of its name; all its overloads by the same Rexx method, which gets the arguments of each call (Write of a TextWriter gets a char, a string, a char[]...).
A property's getter is the method Name, its setter the method "NAME=", as Rexx sends o~Name and o~Name = v.
init, uninit and unknown never override anything.
Members without a Rexx method keep the base's implementation. An abstract one throws NotImplementedException when .NET calls it ("MYCLASS does not define AREA, which the abstract ... needs").

section.para: .NET calls an override as it calls a handler (): at once, on the thread it calls from, the result converted to the member's return type; a Rexx error is a RexxException in .NET, raised again as it was if it comes back to Rexx, and reported on .error where no Rexx code waits. The methods are looked at when extend runs: a method that the class gets later (define) is not an override.

example.title: A Rexx class extending a .NET class
example.programlisting:
c = .Shouting~new c~Add("hello"); c~Insert(0, "world") say c[0] c[1] c~Count c~stored say .net~typeOf(c)
::requires "net.cls" ::class Shouting subclass NetObject ::method activate class -- when the class is created .net~extend(self, "System.Collections.ObjectModel.Collection<System.String>") ::method InsertItem -- protected virtual void InsertItem(int index, string item) use arg index, item self~InsertItem:super(index, item~upper) ::method stored -- Items: a protected property return self~Items~Count "items"

section.para: An interface alone is enough for .NET code that wants one, and the object comes back from .NET as itself, the Rexx object with its class and its state:

example.title: A Rexx class implementing a .NET interface
example.programlisting:
.net~extend(.ByLength, "System.Collections.Generic.IComparer<System.String>") list = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<System.String>")~new do w over "ccc a bb dddd"~makeArray(" "); list~Add(w); end cmp = .ByLength~new list~Sort(cmp) say list~ToArray~makeString("L", " ") held = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<System.Object>")~new held~Add(cmp) say (held[0] == cmp) held[0]~class~id
::requires "net.cls" ::class ByLength subclass NetObject ::method Compare use arg a, b return sign(a~length - b~length)

section.title: Construction
section.para: .MyClass~new(args...) makes the .NET object with the base's constructor (public or protected) that takes the arguments. The object is made first, its Rexx object attached to it, and only then the constructor runs: a base constructor that calls a virtual member (Windows Forms' do) reaches the Rexx method, and that method can use the object. So a class's own init sets what its overrides need, and then calls self~init:super(args...) with the base constructor's arguments. .net~new(type) of the new type is refused (it would have no Rexx object); .NET code that makes one itself gets an object whose overrides run the base's implementations.

section.title: Protected Members, base. and :super
section.para: As in C#, the object's own methods, and only they, reach the base's protected members: self~Items, self~Label = "x". They are private Rexx methods of the class, so ooRexx itself keeps any other code from calling them: from outside, the name is not found (SYNTAX 97.1), as C#'s "inaccessible". Proxies of other .NET objects never see protected members.

As in any Rexx class, self~Name:super(args) is the base's: the implementation of a member the class overrides (C#'s base.Name(args)), or a protected member that the class hides with a method of the same name. self~base.Name(args) does the same for an overridden member ("BASE.NAME=" for a setter).

section.title: Generic Methods, ref and out, Events
section.para: Generic methods. The Rexx method of an overridden generic method gets the type arguments after its arguments, as NetTypes: T Make<T>(string s) is use arg s, t. self~base.Name(args..., types...) passes them on, or they are inferred from the arguments as in any call.

Parameters by reference. A ref or out parameter arrives as a Rexx.Net.ComRef: ref~Value is its value, and ref~Value = x gives the caller a new one. The base's own ref and out parameters take NetRefs, as any .NET call.

Interfaces' events. An event of an interface (INotifyPropertyChanged.PropertyChanged, which WPF's binding listens to) is an event of the new type: .NET code and Rexx code (o~PropertyChanged += handler) subscribe to it, and the object's own methods raise it with self~raise.PropertyChanged(self, args), a private method; with no handlers, nothing happens.

example.title: An interface's event, raised by a Rexx class
example.programlisting:
p = .Person~new p~PropertyChanged += .net~handler(.Watcher~new, "CHANGED") p~setName("Ann") p~setName("Bob") say .net~isInstance(p, "System.ComponentModel.INotifyPropertyChanged")
::requires "net.cls" ::class Person subclass NetObject ::method activate class .net~extend(self, "System.ComponentModel.INotifyPropertyChanged") ::method setName expose name use arg name args = .net~System~ComponentModel~PropertyChangedEventArgs~new("Name") self~raise.PropertyChanged(self, args) ::method name expose name return name ::class Watcher ::method changed use arg sender, e say e~PropertyName "is now" sender~name
example.screen: Name is now Ann Name is now Bob 1

example.title: One Rexx method for every overload
example.programlisting:
w = .Collector~new console = .net~System~Console old = console~Out console~SetOut(w) -- .NET's Console writes to the Rexx object console~WriteLine("from .NET's Console") console~Write("two"); console~Write(" parts"); console~WriteLine console~SetOut(old) say "collected:" w~lines~makeString("L", " | ")
::requires "net.cls" ::class Collector subclass NetObject ::method activate class .net~extend(self, "System.IO.TextWriter") ::attribute lines get ::method init expose lines buffer lines = .array~new; buffer = "" self~init:super ::method Encoding -- abstract in TextWriter: a property return .net~System~Text~Encoding~UTF8 ::method Write -- every virtual Write overload calls this expose lines buffer use arg x -- here: a string, a char, or a char[] if x~isA(.NetArray) then x = x~makeString("C") buffer ||= x~changeStr("0d"x, "") do while buffer~pos("0a"x) > 0 parse var buffer line "0a"x buffer lines~append(line) end

section.title: Lifetime
section.para: Each instance is a pair, the Rexx object and its .NET object, which lives while Rexx holds the one or .NET holds the other. The bridge lets both garbage collectors release it, with nothing to do by hand: while Rexx holds the Rexx object, it holds the .NET object; when Rexx no longer does, the .NET object is held weakly, and the Rexx object is kept for it; when .NET collects the .NET object, the pair is over. Going back to Rexx makes Rexx hold it again. The class's uninit, if it has one, runs once, when the pair is over: when .NET has collected its object, or when the interpreter instance ends (with the overrides still reaching it). The .NET type that extend made is kept by the Rexx class; a class made at run time (.NetObject~subclass(...)), extended, is collected with its type once nothing holds the class or its instances.
On Windows, a Form whose OnPaint, OnResize and ProcessDialogKey are Rexx methods is the project's samples/windows/forms-extend.rex.
